t: Leaders Who Need to Turn Off Their Relentless Focus
q: Leaders who are highly driven to learn and excel sometimes can become hypervigilant about everything in their world.
Those who maintain a never-ending level of awareness and arousal often have a difficult time relaxing even when they are “off duty.
It is no surprise that leaders who are hypervigilant have difficulty maintaining relationships and often experience severe mental health issues.
If they can’t turn off and enjoy themselves, they can be especially difficult to work or live with.
Better is to push these leaders to meditation, yoga, and experiences that require complete disengagement and provide a connection to other people.
Who knew that, for some leaders, turning off is the biggest challenge they face?

t: When to Accept Differences in Views and When to Stand Your Ground
q: Good leaders make it a point to occasionally lose arguments, to be outvoted by the team, and to concede to the wisdom of others whenever they can.
Leaders who “get it” defer to the subject-matter expertise of those team members who are true experts on the issues at hand.
But good leaders stand their ground when it comes to the vision, mission, and values of the organization or team.
Leaders who mistakenly allow the team to have an undue influence over the vision and values of the organization relinquish their role as the leader.
The best leaders concede that they don’t have to have their way on many of the decisions critical for executing strategy.
Sometimes, winning the argument is how to lose the team. But the vision, mission, and values of the team are never up for grabs.

t: Shaping How Others Define Success
q: A recent Gallup survey asked Americans about their view of success.
It is more than curious that people believe others define success very differently than they do.
Fighting the temptation of allowing society to define success is not easy for even the strongest of leaders, but it is essential for your leadership to do so.
Good leaders purposely talk about big-picture abstractions like visions, excellence, and success.
Homogenized thinking is always of a lower quality and is often wrongheaded.

t: The Leadership Ratio That Matters Most
q: The most important ratio for a leader is not debt to equity, supervisor to employee, efficiency to cost, or price to earnings.
The ratio that matters most for leadership success is the proportion of praise to criticism.
Too much criticism and not enough encouragement, and people feel overwhelmed by the expectations and disappointment leaders project.
Study the best leaders in virtually any arena of leadership and you will find a ratio of praise to criticism of roughly 5-to-1.
As marriage guru John Gottman has shown, this ratio even predicts satisfaction between intimate partners.
Five parts encouragement to one part advice gets the job done best.

t: #57 Don't Give the Correct Answer Until After Your Explanation
q: In both scenarios, the teacher confirmed the correct answer before hearing a student's explanation or sharing their own explanation. I think this is a missed opportunity.

Sure, you might be motivated to listen to the explanation to find out how to answer the question correctly, but you might also think: okay, so there is yet another thing I don’t get, and promptly switch off.
Or might you conclude that seeing as you got the question correct, you have earned a little cognitive break, which might result in you missing a critical insight from the teacher or another student?
Either way, confirming the correct answer before an explanation risks incentivising students to switch off from that explanation.
Holding the correct answer back until you have heard from several students (remembering to Hide your Tell, of course!) or until you have finished your explanation does the opposite.

t: Three Tips for More MEANINGful Parent/Teacher Conferences
q: P/T conferences can be the scariest or most frustrating part of the year for a teacher, OR they can be among the most enlightening parts. So much of that is based on what we bring to the conferences.

IF we view P/T conferences as a chance to meet new people, learn more about our students, and gain insight into what our teaching practice looks like from outside our four walls, THEN we'll likely find them an enlightening opportunity.
Probably the best thing goals do for us, motivation-wise, is they define success
But goals can really cause us overwhelm and pressure if we're always setting them high. Yerkes-Dodson called it — us humans can only take so much pressure.
We can focus on the fact that there are going to be parents and guardians and students there tonight who really. Need. Something.
A word of encouragement, someone to listen to them, a solution to the overwhelm THEY are feeling, a reassurance that school is a place where their child's long-term flourishing is being cultivated.

t: Prime Important Meetings With Prework
q: Important meetings, where decisions are made and strategies set, need to be primed for success.
In the ideal design, the meeting starts the moment the invitation goes out and the calendar is set.
Prework is never busy work. It should be designed to get the juices and ideas flowing.
Leaders detest herding people who resist and say they are too busy, so they often hit the eject button and give up on what they know would be a highly additive exercise.
On better teams, the prework is the entry ticket to attend the meeting, no matter who you are or what status you hold on the team.
True meeting success occurs when preparation meets discussion.

Following through on the little things as defined by your classroom management plan keep the big things from ever happening.

t: Raising the Aspirations of Those Who Are Better Than They Think
q: Some team members and colleagues are better than they think they are.
Good leaders don’t accept the low bar these team members have placed on themselves.
The best leaders describe in vivid detail who they see in front of them, why they believe in this person’s talents, and what success they expect this individual to achieve.
Leaders who work to raise the aspirations of valued colleagues can have a life-altering impact on their future.
In the words of a consummate performer and artist, “The greatest danger for most of us is not that our aim is too high and we miss it, but that it is too low and we reach it.

t: Good Memorization, Bad Memorization
q: To me, memorization means knowing something without having to think about it. My goal as a teacher is to pick out all the little pieces of knowledge that my students need when they're solving complex problems.

Memorization is powerful when that knowledge is useful in lots of different places; memorizing something that’s only useful in a narrow context isn’t a good use of time and probably isn’t going to stick anyway.
Teachers forget about them because we have them memorized, so we don't have to think about them! Walk into a typical 7th grade class that's learning about circles.
The quadratic formula is the opposite of the type of thing that's helpful to memorize.

I give a quick five-question retrieval practice Do Now at the start of each class for students to practice stuff I want them to memorize. Each question comes up a bunch of times at increasing intervals.

t: Does Mind-Wandering Harm Learning?
q: First: unsurprisingly (to me), students who mind-wandered remembered less. And, crucially, they remembered less both right away and AND a week later.
Second: surprisingly (to me), the students' interest level didn't matter. That is: even the students who REALLY LIKE DINOS didn't learn as much if they mind-wandered.
Third: horrifyingly (to me), students lose focus roughly 25% of the time.
If we want students to learn 100% of the material, and they’re mentally elsewhere for 25% of the time…well, that distraction puts a firm cap on what they can learn.
Second: check for understanding even more frequently than we might think necessary. Doing so will a) help us know if they are mind-wandering, and b) help keep them focused.

t: Correcting Your Leader Is Best Done by Asking for Clarity Instead
q: When the leader above you makes a mistake, says the wrong thing in a group or client setting, or grossly misreads a situation, it is imperative that they understand the potential consequences and stand ready to make a correction.
Leaders can sometimes overreact to being corrected, as they often find it embarrassing or as a sign they are being disrespected.
One avenue is not to correct the leader or point out the blunder, but to ask them to clarify instead.

Presuming the leader has a reason or logic behind what they did, asking them to clarify and help you learn through the explanation will often unearth the truth that indeed a mistake was made that needs to be corrected.
Correcting your leader can sometimes be risky. Getting curious and taking the more indirect path to raise the issue is often the best call.
As any martial arts master will tell you, the strongest move isn’t always engaging your opponent head-on.

t: How to Create More Buy-In
q: The true source of power for a leader is not authority but buy-in.
How to create more buy-in is the master skill of great leadership.
Without buy-in, even a great decision or strategy is abandoned by the team and only realizes a small part of its full potential.
They are quick to demonstrate their own buy-in before asking others to do so, often going to great lengths to showcase their conviction in group settings.
People get on board slow-moving trains where leaders ask them to collaborate to build a railroad.
They don’t sell or direct. They involve and collaborate. And buy-in is the result.

t: Achieving Outcome Independence During Performance
q: Perhaps the hardest mental contest to win during performance is executing without thought or consideration of the outcome.
Achieving outcome independence is what makes performers great. Yet, this is both largely unknown and underappreciated.
By focusing on the score, outcome, or end result, performers become incapable of staying in the present.
The truth is that performers influence but never control or dictate the outcome or end result.

t: How to Resolve Pop-Up Debate Power Struggles Where a Student Refuses to Speak -to-speak
q: When there is a lull in a pop-up debate, I am quick to call on students who have not yet spoken. I do this to save instructional time, to limit unhelpful awkwardness, and to reduce unhelpful pressure.
I make a note on my clipboard to remind me to touch base with the student — usually just an underline or a 0. I then move on to calling the next person who hasn't spoken yet.
Well, for today's debate, you didn't get any credit, but that's okay — we'll be having another one next week. My question to you is, what can I do to help you make that debate a success?
Well first of all, I think it's the best way because it reduces shame. Most of us experience some degree of anxiety in speaking for our peers. For some of us, this anxiety is debilitating.

I know that, whenever you mix shame in with anxiety, it's a toxic and living cocktail that feeds upon itself. So, by moving on quickly from the refusal to speak, I'm giving shame as little sunlight as possible.

The last thing you want to do for someone who is refusing to speak publicly is place more pressure to speak upon them. And when we turn situations like these into anything other than what I've described above, that's what we do: we increase pressure and shame.

Increasing pressure on a non-speaking student is the wrong move — normalizing setbacks for the rest of the class and giving the student a second chance next week is what eventually gets reluctant speakers participating.

His method: quickly and calmly move on during the debate itself to avoid a public power struggle, then privately pull the student aside afterward to ask what happened, offer help, and invite them to try again next time…

t: #55 Hide Your Tell When Calling Upon Students to Explain Their Thinking
q: So, if you are a teacher who always goes to a student with the correct answer first, then anyone with a different answer immediately knows they are wrong and may not be willing to share their thinking when called upon.
Likewise, if you are a teacher who always saves the correct answer to last, anyone called upon first will know they are wrong and may also be reluctant to share their thoughts.

In both scenarios, there is also the issue of any student who has the correct answer immediately knowing they are correct and so tuning out of the explanations of students who have a different answer to them.
So, with a multiple-choice diagnostic question, I always pick a student who has chosen option A first, regardless if it is right or wrong, followed by B, then C, then D.

This simple technique means my students do not know whether they are right or wrong simply based on the order I choose them, so are more willing to share their reasoning, and have an extra incentive to keep listening.

t: Rehearsal in PD
q: Rehearsal is when we practise a change to our teaching outside the classroom, either on our own or (even better) with the support of a colleague or coach.

Making a change to our teaching requires the repeated co-ordination of novel sequences of thought, speech, posture, and more—all at once. The classroom is already a highly cognitively demanding environment.

t: #54 Ask Students Not to Say or Write Anything for 30 Seconds
q: A potential solution is asking students not to say or write anything for 30 seconds. Instead, they are to think about the problem.
We might ask students not to say anything because it prevents the reflex response of “I don’t get it” whenever students are faced with anything unfamiliar.
It prevents them from diving in head first without properly reading the question. It allows them to plot a route through the problem.
In the language of psychologist Daniel Kahneman, those 30 seconds give our students’ more thoughtful System 2s a chance to override their more instinctual, but often faulty, System 1s.

When you first introduce this approach, you are likely to be met by resistance. Those 30 seconds will feel like 3 hours, and students will be desperate to ask you questions or to write something down.
And when students start to notice the benefit of those 30 seconds of calm contemplation, especially in exams, most should jump on board.

t: How I Use Worked Examples

The goal of a worked example isn’t just to show students an example, it’s to simplify the learning experience so there are fewer demands on the student’s attention and working memory.
I ask students to read the problem and the solution and try to understand what’s happening. Sometimes I’ll add a few quick pieces of clarification as well.
There’s nothing to copy down and not much else happening on the page. I keep the solution as simple as possible.
